ABSTRACT
The US Environmental Protection Agency recently released strict regulations limiting per- and polyfluoroalkyl 
substances (PFAS) in drinking water. In response, this study used activated carbons derived from biomass waste 
components for effective water treatment. By varying the composition of feedstock mixtures, perfluorobutane 
sulfonic acid adsorption efficiencies ranged from 31 to 98 %, indicating that biomass structure influences PFAS 
sorption. Activated carbon from a feedstock mixture of 50 % lignin, 35 % cellulose nanocrystals, and 15 % 
cellulose nanofibers achieved over 98 % removal of three regulated and four unregulated PFAS compounds 
without requiring additives or surface functionalization.
1. Introduction
The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) recently introduced 
regulations aimed at reducing exposure to six per- and polyfluoroalkyl 
substances (PFAS), commonly known as “ forever chemicals, ” in drinking 
water [1] . These guidelines are expected to benefit 100 million people, 
preventing thousands of deaths and many PFAS-related illnesses. To 
meet these regulations, utilities are exploring granular activated carbon 
(AC) to remove PFAS from water sources.
Agricultural residues, which accumulate and contribute to environ -
mental and health hazards, offer a sustainable and abundant source for 
producing AC [2,3] . This biomass is mainly comprised of lignin and 
cellulose, both of which have been shown to contribute to the formation 
of the AC structure [4] . However, the relationship between biomass 
components on AC structure and their effectiveness as PFAS sorbents has 
yet to be fully understood. This research aims to fill this gap by inves -
tigating how the structure of AC derived from lignin (LIG) and cellulose 
influences their PFAS adsorption efficiency. The investigation includes 
an initial screening experiment to identify the most effective AC derived 
from LIG, cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs), and cellulose nanofibers (CNFs) 
for adsorbing short-chain PFAS. Once the best-performing AC was 
identified, experiments were repeated to understand the material ’ s 
adsorption behavior on seven common PFAS.
2. Materials and methods
PFAS compounds were selected to include anionic (PFBA, PFBS, 
PFOA, and PFOS), zwitterionic (6:2 FTAB), and cationic (PFHxSAmS 
and PFOSAmS) species with varying chain lengths to understand PFAS 
structure-dependent adsorption by AC. Further details of each model 
PFAS are presented in Table S1. Feedstock biomass characterization 
results using previously established methods [4] are provided in 
Table S2.
Eight mixtures of biomass components were chosen to create a range 
of surface areas (SSA) and microporosity. AC were prepared as described 
previously [4] and named using the system listed in Table 1 AC-5 was 
duplicated in this work to understand batch-to-batch variations. In 
addition to the nine AC samples described, a common wood biochar was 
activated using the same protocol. This compares the adsorption effi -
ciency of tailored AC to AC produced from currently available biochar. 
The SSA and micropore analysis were measured on a Micromeritics 
TriStar II 3020 using BET analysis, surface charge of the best AC was 
determined using zeta potential, and elemental analysis was conducted 
using x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). More details on BET 
sample preparation and analysis techniques can be found in Supple -
mentary Material.

Abstract. Cigarette butts (CB s) are among the most abundant forms of anthropogenic litter worldwide and constitute a per-
sistent source of environmental contamination due to their slow degradation and the release of toxic substances into terrestrial
and aquatic ecosystems. In this review, we critically evaluate recent advances in the valorisation of CB  waste into value-
added functional materials. Particular attention is given to conversion strategies includ-ing chemical activation, electrospin -
ning, hydrothermal processing and nanocomposite fabrication. These approaches enable the production of activated carbons,
cellulose-derived na-nomaterials and metal-doped composites with promising applications in water purification, energy stor-
age, vector control and pollutant remediation. W e discuss the underlying mechanisms, performance, scalability and sustain -
ability of these technologies, and highlight current challenges, research gaps and future opportunities of large-scale imple -
mentation. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that CB s can be re-envisioned as valuable secondary resources that support
circular economy and sustainable material development strategies.

Keywords: activated carbon | carbon yield | crosslinking degree | phenolic resin | porous carbon | supercapacitor 
ABSTRACT 
Porous carbons are indispensable for supercapacitors and as hosts for silicon anodes in next-generation lithium-ion batteries, 
yet their commercialization is crippled by the low carbon yield of phenolic resin precursors. What fundamentally controls the 
yield and how to improve it have long puzzled both academia and industry. Here, we address the root cause by systematically 
tuning the formaldehyde-to-phenol (F/P) molar ratio. We discover that the methylene bridge density in the cured resin is the key 
determinant of carbon yield. At the optimal F/P ratio of 2.0, the resin achieves the most complete crosslinked network, boosting 
the porous carbon yield from below 36% (PC-1.0) to 47.15% (PC-2.0), without compromising pore development. PC-2.0 retains a 
high specific surface area of 2580.6 m2 ⋅g− 1 and delivers an outstanding specific capacitance of 371.8 F ⋅g− 1 at 0.5 A ⋅g− 1 . Moreover, 
it exhibits a high capacitance retention of 95.76% after 10 000 cycles at a current density of 10 A ⋅g− 1 , demonstrating competitive 
advantages over various electrode materials reported in recent years. Quantitative analysis confirms a strong positive correlation 
between methylene content and yield, solving the long-standing puzzle. This work provides a simple, scalable strategy to break 
the yield-performance trade-off, reducing raw material cost by 16.47% compared with commercial resin.

as well as biofuel-based energy conversion devices [ 16 ]. In many 
of these systems, porous carbons, owing to their high specific 
surface area (SSA), tunable pore structure, excellent electrical 
conductivity, and good chemical/thermal stability, demonstrate

in supercapacitors, delivering high power density and ultra- 
long cycle life [ 20 ], and additionally acts as an excellent host 
for silicon-based anodes, mitigating the volume expansion dur- 
ing charge/discharge processes, among other applications [ 21 ].

Unveiling the energy storage potential of valorized 
unripe plantain peel-derived activated carbon
Ayesha Samrin · Mohammed Rehaan Chandan · Igor Levchenko · Katia Alexander  ·

Abstract
The damage from excess waste generation on the environment has made it necessary to re-think how we 
approach product development and the waste management lifecycle. Within this framework, conversion of 
biowaste into energy storage materials has emerged as an effective means of reducing the environmental 
impact of food production. In this work, activated car-bon with superior supercapacitive properties is produced 
directly from unripe plantain peel by optimizing the use of two different activating agents KOH and ZnCl 2 dur-
ing pyrolysis. Activated carbon Z7 which was pyrolyzed at 700 °C using ZnCl 2 as the activating agent had a 
higher sur-face area of 1636 m 2/g and higher electrochemical performance when compared to activated carbon 
produced under all other experimental conditions. The specific capacitance obtained for Z7 in a two-electrode 
Swagelok set-up was 167 F g −1 at 0.5 A/g and an excellent energy density of 23 Wh/kg at a power density of 
174 W/kg at 0.5 A/g current was obtained. Further-more, a capacitance retention of 79% was achieved after 
4500 cycles at a current density of 5 A/g with a coulombic efficiency of 99%.
Keywords Unripe plantain peels · KOH and ZnCl 2 activation · Porosity · Specific capacitance
Introduction
Driven by the growing population and its increasing use of energy-intensive technologies, the global consump -
tion of energy continues to increase, at a significant cost to the environment. To slow down the depletion of fos-
sil fuels, and reduce associated emissions, there have been significant global efforts to transition to clean forms 
of energy, with a particularly strong focus on renewable energy sources, such as solar or wind. However, their 
intermittent nature as well as potential asynchronicity between peak generation and peak demand necessitates the 
development of efficient systems for energy storage, such as batteries, flywheels, supercapacitors. Supercapaci -
tor is an efficient energy storage system due to its high-power density and high stability. The energy is stored 
in a supercapacitor by two mechanisms, namely (i) Electric double layer (EDLC) and (ii) Faradaic redox reac -
tions. For a clean energy storage system, the electric double layer capacitor (EDLC) materials are highly suitable 
as they are potentially sustainable, have a longer life cycle, chemically stable and are also economical [ 6, 36].

supercapacitor electrode synthesis 
and evaluation
Amany Mostafa1, Sodky H. Mohammed2, Nouby M. Ghazaly1 & Ahmed ElSheikh 1
Climate and energy issues continue to drive researchers to develop fossil-free energy technologies that 
are both sustainable and scalable. In this work, date seeds (DS) are used to produce activated carbon 
(DSAC), which is then used as a supercapacitor electrode. The synthesis method uses KOH activation 
coupled with argon-gas flow calcination at 950 °C. The produced DSAC has a high specific surface area 
of 1374 m2/g and a turbostratic microporous structure (pore size = 1.14 nm), in addition to oxygen-
containing functional groups (–C–O–, –OH). The DSAC electrochemical performance exhibits an electric 
double-layer capacitor (EDLC) with a minor pseudocapacitive contribution and delivers a 3-electrode 
specific capacitance of 1800 F/g at 4 A/g (estimated full-device specific capacitance is 450 F/g, energy, 
and power densities: 40 Wh/kg and 1440 W/kg, respectively). These numbers are remarkably higher 
than the current state-of-the-art carbon supercapacitor findings. Furthermore, it retains 83.3% of its 
initial discharge capacity after 2000 galvanostatic charge-discharge cycles at 10 A/g. Finally, the DSAC 
electrode performance is slightly enhanced with increasing the KOH concentration from 1 M to 3 M.
Keywords Biomass, Activated carbon, Supercapacitor, KOH activation
The climate change and energy supply crises continue to call for accelerated research and development efforts 
of sustainable energy technologies1. This is particularly true in electric mobility, where supercapacitors and Li-
ion batteries play a vital role. Supercapacitors or electrochemical capacitors are electrochemical cells comprised 
of two electrodes, a separator, and an electrolyte. Their inherent merits, which occasionally enable them to 
outperform Li-ion batteries, include fast charging and discharging, high power density, and long cycle life 2. 
There are two main mechanisms for storing electrical charge in supercapacitors: electric double-layer capacitors 
(EDLCs) and pseudocapacitors. The former adopts the electrostatic adsorption and desorption of electrolyte 
ions at the electrode-electrolyte interface, forming the double-layer configuration. The latter is achieved via a 
reversible redox charge-transfer reaction at the electrode-electrolyte interface. Occasionally, both mechanisms 
occur simultaneously in a single material, combining the advantages of both 3. Furthermore, supercapacitors 
could be classified based on their materials into metal oxide, polymer, and carbon-based. Unlike oxide and 
polymer-based supercapacitors, carbon-based supercapacitors have demonstrated stable performance in 
addition to their cost-effectiveness4.
Biomass-based electrodes have garnered considerable attention due to their inherent properties, such 
as raw material abundance, high surface area, chemical stability, high specific surface area, low weight, and 
interconnected porous structure5. Wood residues, coconut shells, apricot pits, agricultural wastes, and marine 
algae are some of the examples of biomass precursors that have been extensively studied in the preparation of 
porous activated carbons with well-developed micro/mesoporous structure that can be used in supercapacitor 
applications6–11. The chemical activation process can be used to produce hierarchical porous carbons with a 
large surface area and tunable pore structure using these lignocellulosic resources. Recent research work has 
shown that carbons produced by biomass have the potential to provide promising electrochemical properties 
when optimized activation conditions are used and thus can serve as sustainable alternatives to standard carbon 
materials. As an example, it has been reported that porous carbons obtained using many natural precursors as 
hydrogen storage and energy-related materials have been investigated in the past, thus showing the success of the 
chemical activation strategies in the development of pore structure and surface chemistry12,13.

ABSTRACT
Biomass-derived carbon materials represent stable, cost-effective and environmentally friendly electrocatalyst for 
oxygen evolution reaction (OER) and hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). In this work, a self-supporting coconut 
shell carbon (SCC) catalyst featuring a three-dimensional (3D) hierarchical porous structure was reported by in 
situ ammonia etching. The SCC-1100-NH
3 
exhibited outstanding OER performance, achieving a current density 
of 10 mA cm
� 2 
at an overpotential of 294 mV and a potential of 1.52 V vs RHE. The unique structural config -
uration also offered the catalyst excellent durability with stable operation for at least 98 h. It was believed that 
the hierarchical porous structure enhances electrical conductivity and the formation of vacancy-coupled 
pentagon defects which act as active sites. This work provides a new strategy for designing defect-rich metal- 
free biomass-derived carbon electrodes.
1. Introduction
Oxygen evolution reaction (OER) is a critical process in renewable 
energy technologies, yet its practical application is hindered by intrin -
sically slow kinetics involving a four-electron transfer, which leads to 
high overpotentials ( η > 200 mV) [ 1 – 3 ]. This inefficiency remains a key 
obstacle in devices such as electrolysers, regenerative fuel cells and 
metal-air batteries. Although noble metal oxides (e.g., IrO
2 
and RuO
2
) 
represent the state-of-the-art OER catalysts due to their high activity and 
stability [ 4 ], their high cost and limited availability impede widespread 
use [ 2 , 5 ]. Moreover, under harsh oxidizing conditions, these catalysts 
often suffer from dissolution or surface reconstruction, further under -
mining their long-term stability. These challenges have motivated the 
search for cost-effective and durable alternatives. Metal-free carbon- 
based materials such as biomass-derived carbons, graphene and carbon 
nanotubes [ 6 ], have gained increasing attentions because of low cost, 
tunable electronic properties, high stability, and the use of earth- 
abundant precursors.
The OER on metal-free carbon catalysts operates through a mecha -
nism fundamentally different from that of conventional metal-based 
oxides [ 7 ]. Instead of relying on metal d-orbitals, the catalytic activity 
stems from modifications to the electronic structure of the carbon 
framework. Heteroatom doping with elements such as nitrogen, boron, 
phosphorus and sulfur, enables precise redistribution of charge within 
the carbon matrix. For instance, pyridinic nitrogen provides lone elec -
tron pairs, while graphitic nitrogen enhances conjugation, and both ef -
fects promote charge polarization to form highly active sites that may 
act synergistically to improve electrocatalytic performance [ 8 – 12 ]. 
Notably, engineered carbon defects can exhibit higher catalytic efficacy 
than even pyridinic-N sites in certain doped graphitic carbons [ 13 ], 
establishing defects as emerging active centers in carbon-based elec -
trocatalysis. Structural imperfections such as vacancies, edges and to -

electron density and creating regions of enhanced charge that favor the
